title: Can YOU solve this? Reflections 🧠 #SATPrep #Shorts
description:
#SATPrep #Shorts #SAT
🎓 SAT Prep Quiz: Reflections
🎨 Theme: Mission to Mars

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
QUESTIONS IN THIS REEL
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Q1. The parabola y = x^2 + 1 is reflected across the line x = 0. What is the equation of the reflected parabola?
✅ Answer: B. y = -x^2 + 1
💡 When the graph of a function is reflected across the line x = 0 (y-axis), the x values are negated. However, since x^2 remains the same for both positive and negative x, the reflection of y = x^2 + 1 across x = 0 is y = (-x)^2 + 1, which simplifies to y = x^2 + 1. But in this case, considering the nature of reflection across the y-axis, we should look at how the function behaves with -x. Thus, the equation becomes y = (-x)^2 + 1, which indeed simplifies to y = x^2 + 1. Yet, for a proper reflection across the y-axis in terms of function transformation, we consider the equation in terms of y = f(-x), which for the given equation does not change due to the x^2 term. However, my initial interpretation missed the mark on explaining the transformation correctly in relation to common function transformations. The correct interpretation should focus on how x^2 does not change with the sign of x, thus the equation after reflection across the y-axis remains y = x^2 + 1. Yet, considering standard transformation rules and to correct the step: reflecting y = x^2 + 1 across the y-axis (x=0) gives us y = (-x)^2 + 1, which indeed is y = x^2 + 1. The error was in overcomplicating the explanation and not directly stating that for the given equation, reflection across the y-axis does not change the equation due to the nature of x^2 being the same for positive and negative x.

Q2. The graph of the circle (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 4 is reflected across the line y = 1. What is the equation of the reflected circle?
✅ Answer: A. (x - 1)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 4
💡 To reflect a circle across a horizontal line, we change the sign of the y-coordinate of the center and adjust it according to the line of reflection. So, (1, 2) becomes (1, 0) because |2 - 1| = 1, then we have (1, -1 + 2) which gives (1, 1), but considering the nature of reflection and adjusting, it should be (x - 1)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 4.

7x + 2 = 37

title: Why the chorus in Come Monday is so cool, a Jimmy Buffett harmony lesson
description:
Harmony, chords, and melody are not just sterile music theory—they are how a songwriter makes songs cool and memorable. In this video you’ll see and hear how Jimmy Buffett did it in one of his “Big 8” hits: Come Monday.  


TRANSCRIPT 
0:00
[Jay Albert of Songdog Music singing and playing guitar on the chorus of Come Monday by Jimmy Buffett, stopping right at the lyric “four lonely days”, creating an interruption purposely.]

And right now, if you know this classic by Jimmy Buffett, you are saying “DUDE, finish it!”

I will.
But my purpose in this vid is to share with you why that chorus is such a great hook.

0:25
There is momentum there and a big part of that is the chord changes.
The overall musical term for this is Harmony. It refers to chords, key, chord changes, and melody, all interacting together. 

The verses of Come Monday are pretty standard, I IV V stuff. 

0:46
[Jay demonstrating on guitar the I, IV, and V chords in A major, as used in the verse of Come Monday.]
A is the I chord, D is the IV chord, E is V.
The chorus is where it really gets interesting though, it starts off continuing with the I IV V. 

0:59 
But then he throws in the iii chord, it’s a C# minor 7th, and it gives such a pop of color there.

Jimmy pushes the momentum, not just with that surprise chord, he also changes from chord to chord twice as quickly as he did in the verse.
I  iii IV V

1:18 
[Jay playing guitar while speaking lyrics for reference and analyzing chord changes. “four lonely days in a brown L.A. haze”, ]


That is just superb!
That sequence of chords gives the impression of a rising line.
Meanwhile the vocal is descending in this plaintive, beautiful melody. 

1:34
That contrast
which features the unexpected C#m7 chord
Creates this strong motion and gorgeous counterpoint.
You put that all together and that’s what makes the chorus so tight and gorgeous in this song. One of the reasons, I think, it’s such a popular song. 

Watch the Related video where I play a cover of the final chorus; 
you’ll hear and feel how satisfying all of this sounds when Jimmy and I put it together.

title: Compose Effective Chord Progressions… even if you don’t know theory (Counterpoint for Composers)
description:
▶ Start the free course: https://www.uremusic.com/audiation-inner-ear-training-for-musicians How to write counterpoint in four voices — all five species, applied to the SATB ensemble that sits underneath almost every chorale, fugue, and orchestral score in Western music. Full course here: https://www.uremusic.com/counterpoint-for-composers

🎹 Piano Volume: The piano in this recording is intentionally mixed low, as this course is meant to be taken after developing audiation skills. Don't turn up your speakers — instead, use what you hear as a starting point and try to complete the sound internally. That internal hearing is the skill we're building. 

This is Lecture 12 of Counterpoint for Composers, a 24‑lecture course for writers who already have two‑ and three‑part species under their belt. We start with why four parts are the foundational texture — the “conversation among four people” analogy runs through the whole lesson — then move into the mechanics: the six voice‑pairs you must check on every beat, SATB ranges and spacing, doubling, and the leading‑tone trap.

From there we walk species by species:
• First species (note‑against‑note)
• Second species (two‑against‑one with passing tones)
• Third species (four‑against‑one)
• Fourth species (suspensions, including the chain — one of the most beautiful sounds in tonal music)
• Fifth species (florid)

We close with combining species across voices, voice independence, texture and balance, an eight‑step writing workflow, and two complete worked examples — one with the cantus in the bass, one with the cantus in the soprano.

By the end, you’ll have a reliable workflow for writing four‑part counterpoint and the error‑checking habits to keep it clean.

title: The Raise Trap: Why Earning More Makes You Broke | The Math Proves It
description:
That 15% raise was supposed to change your life. It didn’t. Personal Finance Basics reveals why — and why most people stay stuck for decades despite earning more.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracked thousands of households — and found something brutal: income goes up, spending follows almost perfectly. Personal Finance Basics calls this the Parallel Line Paradox — where your lifestyle rises just fast enough to cancel your progress.
Tom and Nina got the same 15% raise. Same job. Same path. But 30 years later, Nina is worth $2.4 million more. Personal Finance Basics shows the real difference wasn’t income — it was one simple rule applied consistently.
Most people fall into the Raise Trap without realizing it. Personal Finance Basics breaks down how every raise quietly locks you into higher fixed costs — until your future income is already spent.
No apps. No extreme budgeting. Just math. Personal Finance Basics explains the Fifty Percent Rule and the Lifestyle Lag Strategy — systems that stop your income from disappearing the moment it arrives.

title: Photography Tips for Beginner Photographers Tip 1#photographytips #beginnerphotography #photography
description:
As a beginner photographer do you avoid manual mode because it feels too complicated? 📸

Most beginner photographers avoid manual mode like the plague. They stay on auto, watch more tutorials, and wonder why their photos aren't improving. 

But after 15 years working as a cinematographer and photographer this is the first thing I tell every single person I teach.

Manual mode is the fastest shortcut to understanding your camera.

Every overexposed shot, every blurry image, every photo that comes out too dark your camera is not failing you. It's teaching you. That's the exposure triangle in action. Shutter speed, aperture and ISO working together and the quickest and most effective way to truly understand how they relate to each other is to get them wrong again and again  on manual mode.

No course. No tutorial. No YouTube video will teach you this faster than twenty minutes outside making mistakes.

The mistake IS the lesson. Trust the process. 📸
